clinical_knowledge.topic: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis is essential for appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.
Clinical history, severity assessment, and targeted testing must be interpreted together rather than relying on one symptom alone.
Treat pulmonary-renal syndrome as an emergency with hospital admission and multidisciplinary input.
Management should follow local pathways and account for patient-specific comorbidity and clinical severity.

Objective/examination findings: Perform focused examination, vital-sign assessment, and diagnosis-specific investigations.

common_misconceptions: Assuming a mild or atypical presentation rules out Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.
Relying on a single normal test result to prematurely exclude serious pathology.
Equating transient symptom improvement with resolution of the underlying condition.
Failing to consider clinically important alternative diagnoses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before appropriate assessment.
Starting treatment without considering contraindications, interactions, or organ function.
Ignoring critical warning signs: Haemoptysis with hypoxaemia.
management_principles: Treat pulmonary-renal syndrome as an emergency with hospital admission and multidisciplinary input.
Confirm the syndrome with urinalysis, renal function, ANCA testing, imaging, and tissue biopsy when safe.
Use remission-induction immunosuppression under specialist guidance and provide infection prophylaxis and monitoring.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 49M presents with 4-month classic pulmonary-renal syndrome: destructive upper airway disease (bloody nasal crusts, saddle nose), lower tract haemoptysis, constitutional decline, and acute glomerulonephritis.
reference_soap.objective: Perform targeted multidisciplinary physical examination. Upper airway/ENT exam: inspect nasal septum -> demonstrates septal perforation and saddle-nose deformity (cartilage collapse), plus bloody mucosal crusting. Auscultation: scattered crackles and wheezes over bilateral lung fields. Dipstick urinalysis: 3+ protein and 3+ blood. Urine microscopy: active nephritic sediment confirming Red Blood Cell Casts and dysmorphic erythrocytes (indicates acute rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). Bloods: serum creatinine rapidly rising (e.g., 280 umol/L confirming acute kidney injury), FBC (normocytic anaemia, leukocytosis), CRP >120. CRITICAL AUTOANTIBODY SEROLOGY: check ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies) -> strongly positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic pattern) with high titre anti-PR3 (Proteinase-3 antibodies >100 IU/mL; pathognomonic for GPA). Check anti-GBM antibodies (negative ruling out Goodpasture's). High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Chest: reveals multiple bilateral lung nodules of varying sizes, many exhibiting central cavitation with thick walls, plus ground-glass opacities indicating diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Urgent Renal Biopsy: demonstrates Pauci-Immune Crescentric Glomerulonephritis (glomerular crescents without immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence).
reference_soap.assessment: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA -> formerly Wegener's Granulomatosis; ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis presenting as severe pulmonary-renal syndrome). DDx: Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA -> p-ANCA / anti-MPO positive, lacks destructive upper airway/granulomatous saddle-nose lesions), Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss -> shows asthma and severe eosinophilia), Goodpasture's Syndrome (Anti-GBM disease -> linear IgG on renal biopsy without upper airway crusting), systemic lupus erythematosus.
reference_soap.plan: This pulmonary-renal presentation requires immediate hospital admission and urgent rheumatology, nephrology, and respiratory input. Assess gas exchange, haemodynamic status, renal function, urinalysis, infection, ANCA and anti-GBM serology, imaging, and obtain tissue diagnosis when safe. The specialist team may initiate remission-induction immunosuppression after evaluating infection and contraindications; critical-care and renal-replacement support may be needed for respiratory failure or severe acute kidney injury.

learning_objectives: Identify the classical pulmonary-renal syndrome triad of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis: upper airway destruction, nodular/cavitating lung lesions, and crescentric glomerulonephritis
Interpret c-ANCA with anti-PR3 specificity and pauci-immune crescentic renal biopsy as supporting GPA in the clinical context
Differentiate GPA from Goodpasture's syndrome and Microscopic Polyangiitis based on upper airway cartilage necrosis and ANCA targets
Recognize the need for urgent specialist-directed remission induction after infection and diagnostic assessment

teaching.one_liner: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing destructive upper-airway disease, pulmonary haemorrhage, and glomerulonephritis.
red_flags: Rapidly worsening kidney function or oliguria

history.answer: I've been coughing up bloody phlegm for four months, and my sinuses are blocked with painful bloody crusts.
The blood comes straight up from my chest when I cough. It's not from vomiting, though I do have separate bloody crusts inside my nose.
I cough up phlegm mixed with dark red blood multiple times every day, about a teaspoonful each time. It has never filled an entire cup.
It's usually dark red or brownish mixed with thick yellowish mucus, sometimes with bright red streaks. There is never any food in it.
I first noticed blood in my phlegm about four months ago. It started as thin streaks but has become more frequent and heavier over the weeks.
I developed a dry hacking cough four months ago that quickly turned into bringing up thick, discolored mucus. It has steadily worsened rather than clearing up.
I bring up thick, yellowish-green foul-smelling phlegm every single day. I haven't had recurrent pneumonia before this started.
I've had low-grade fevers and chills coming and going in the afternoons for the past few weeks. I haven't had severe shaking chills.
I've lost about five kilograms over the past four months without trying, and I wake up drenched in sweat at night. I feel completely exhausted.
I feel a bit winded when climbing stairs, but I haven't had sudden shortness of breath. I don't have sharp, stabbing chest pain when breathing.
history.topic: Shortness of breath and chest pain

history.answer: Neither calf is swollen or painful on one side, and I haven't had recent surgery, prolonged bed rest, or cancer treatment.
I don't get breathless lying flat, and I don't wake up gasping for air. Both of my ankles have become puffy over the last five days, though.
My nose has been completely blocked for four months with painful cheek pressure and foul-smelling, bloody crusts blowing out constantly.
About five days ago, my urine turned a dark, smoky red like cola. My daily urine amount seems slightly less, and my ankles are swollen.
No, I don't have bleeding gums, nosebleeds outside the crusting, or unusual bruising anywhere. I do not take any blood-thinning pills.
No nausea, vomiting, or heartburn at all. My bowel movements look completely normal with no black tarry stools.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I have never had tuberculosis or received treatment for it. To my knowledge, I haven't been in contact with anyone who had tuberculosis.
I haven't traveled overseas recently, and I work indoors as a mechanical engineer without heavy dust or chemical fume exposure.
About three weeks ago, I noticed the bridge of my nose was caving in slightly. It looks sunken and flattened across the middle.
I developed an aching pain and muffled hearing in my right ear three weeks ago. The clinic doctor said there was fluid behind the eardrum.
My knees and wrists have been stiff and aching for several weeks now. I haven't noticed any purple spots, bumps, or rashes on my skin.
Doctors gave me four different courses of antibiotics over the last four months for my sinuses and chest, but none of them helped at all.
I feel like a flesh-eating resistant sinus germ has eroded through my nasal bones and dripped down through my body to infect my kidneys.
I am terrified that this is some aggressive, spreading cancer in my head and neck that has moved into my lungs and is destroying my kidneys.
I was hoping you could run autoimmune blood tests, start me on strong immune treatments, and maybe arrange a kidney biopsy right away.
I've had recurrent bouts of sinus trouble for about a year, and I have mild high blood pressure.
I've never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take paracetamol or ibuprofen occasionally when the facial pain and joint aches get bad. Aside from the failed antibiotic courses, I don't take anything else.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I work as a mechanical engineer at an office and live with my wife in an apartment.
My parents both had mild high blood pressure, but there is no family history of autoimmune disorders, vasculitis, or kidney disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, heart rate 86 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Depressed nasal bridge, anterior septal perforation, and thick friable bloody crusts on nasal mucosa without active oral bleeding.
Moderate bilateral tenderness over maxillary and frontal sinuses.
Right tympanic membrane is erythematous and bulging with middle ear fluid; left tympanic membrane is normal.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Scattered coarse crackles and occasional wheezes audible across bilateral mid and lower lung zones.
Resonant percussion notes throughout bilateral lung fields without focal dullness.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Jugular venous pressure is 2 cm above sternal angle with no jugular venous distension.
Bilateral symmetrical 1+ pitting edema around both ankles; no digital clubbing.
Both calves are soft, non-tender, and symmetrical without swelling or palpable cords.
Mild joint tenderness without warmth or obvious effusion over bilateral knees and wrists.
No palpable purpura, rashes, petechiae, or skin ulcers observed.
